topics.name: War of 1812
topics.kicker: U.S. vs. Britain, 1812–1815 · Gave America its national anthem
topics.briefing: In the War of 1812, the young United States fought Great Britain again, angry that British ships were seizing American sailors and forcing them to serve in the Royal Navy. British troops burned the White House, and the bombardment of Fort McHenry inspired Francis Scott Key to write “The Star-Spangled Banner.” Oddly, the war’s biggest American victory, Andrew Jackson’s win at New Orleans, came after the peace treaty had already been signed.

sample.note: the 8 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: One of this war’s bloodiest battles was fought at Lundy’s Lane, near Niagara Falls, where the American general Winfield Scott was badly wounded. Weeks earlier, Scott’s brigade, wearing gray uniforms because blue cloth was scarce, won the Battle of Chippawa.
tossups.r: Several American invasions of Canada failed during this war. For 10 points, name this war between the United States and Great Britain that ended with the Treaty of Ghent.

tossups.p: During this war, a sudden storm that included a tornado swept through an occupied city, helping put out fires that enemy troops had set, and the troops left soon after. They had marched into that city after routing American militia at Bladensburg, Maryland.
tossups.r: Dolley Madison had a portrait of George Washington rescued before the White House burned. For 10 points, name this war in which the British burned Washington, D.C.

tossups.p: Early in this war, the British general Isaac Brock forced William Hull to surrender Detroit without a battle. Brock was killed two months later while leading a charge at the Battle of Queenston Heights, and he is still honored as a hero in Canada.
tossups.r: Oliver Hazard Perry’s victory on Lake Erie later helped Americans retake Detroit. For 10 points, name this war, fought partly over the British impressment of American sailors.

tossups.p: Before this war, Congress passed Macon’s Bill No. 2, which offered to cut off trade with either Britain or France if the other dropped its limits on American shipping. Napoleon tricked James Madison by pretending to drop France’s limits, and tensions with Britain grew.
tossups.r: “War Hawks” in Congress then demanded a fight with Britain. For 10 points, name this war that ended with the Treaty of Ghent.

tossups.p: In the last major battle of this war, British general Edward Pakenham was killed leading an attack on an American line behind the Rodriguez Canal. Pirates led by Jean Lafitte [“luh-FEET”], free Black militiamen, and Choctaw warriors all helped defend that line.
tossups.r: Andrew Jackson won that battle at New Orleans after the peace treaty had already been signed. For 10 points, name this war between the United States and Britain.

tossups.p: New England Federalists who opposed this war met at the Hartford Convention, which led critics to accuse them of disloyalty. The convention’s demands reached Washington just as news of victory and peace did, and the Federalist Party soon faded away.
tossups.r: Federalists had mocked this conflict as “Mr. Madison’s War.” For 10 points, name this war in which Francis Scott Key wrote “The Star-Spangled Banner.”

tossups.p: Thomas Macdonough’s fleet defeated a British squadron on Lake Champlain in this war, forcing a large British army to retreat from Plattsburgh back into Canada. That victory helped American diplomats get better peace terms.
tossups.r: Weeks earlier, the British had burned the White House. For 10 points, name this war that inspired “The Star-Spangled Banner.”

tossups.p: In 1813, American troops captured York, the capital of Upper Canada, and set fire to its government buildings. That town is now the city of Toronto, and the British later pointed to the raid as a reason for one of their own attacks.
tossups.r: That British attack burned the White House and the Capitol in Washington, D.C. For 10 points, name this war between the young United States and Britain.

tossups.p: After Captain James Lawrence was mortally wounded aboard the frigate _Chesapeake_ in this war, his order “Don’t give up the ship” was sewn onto a battle flag. A young commander carried that flag in a rowboat to a new flagship after his first one was badly damaged.
tossups.r: That commander, Oliver Hazard Perry, then wrote, “We have met the enemy and they are ours.” For 10 points, name this war that included the Battle of Lake Erie.

tossups.p: In one of this war’s first sea battles, the frigate USS _Constitution_ defeated HMS _Guerriere_ [“gair-ee-AIR”], and legend says a sailor cheered that British cannonballs were bouncing off its sides. That victory gave the ship its nickname, “Old Ironsides.”
tossups.r: The British later burned the White House in this war. For 10 points, name this conflict between the United States and Britain that ended in 1815.

tossups.p: During this war, Andrew Jackson defeated the Red Stick Creeks at the Battle of Horseshoe Bend in what is now Alabama, with help from Cherokee and Lower Creek allies. The Treaty of Fort Jackson then forced the Creek Nation to give up about 23 million acres of land.
tossups.r: Jackson later won the Battle of New Orleans. For 10 points, name this war that some called America’s “Second War of Independence.”

tossups.p: The Shawnee leader Tecumseh, who had tried to unite Native nations against American expansion, fought as a British ally in this war. He was killed at the Battle of the Thames [“TEMZ”] in what is now Ontario by forces under William Henry Harrison.
tossups.r: Earlier, Oliver Hazard Perry’s win on Lake Erie had cut British supply lines. For 10 points, name this war fought while James Madison was president.

tossups.p: Henry Clay and John C. Calhoun were leading “War Hawks” who pushed Congress to declare this war. President James Madison’s message to Congress listed British impressment of American sailors and British support for Native attacks on the frontier as reasons to fight.
tossups.r: Many War Hawks hoped to conquer Canada. For 10 points, name this war in which Andrew Jackson became a hero at New Orleans.

tossups.p: Mary Pickersgill and her helpers sewed a giant flag for a fort that was bombarded during this war; that flag is now displayed at the Smithsonian. A lawyer who watched the bombardment from a ship off Baltimore saw the flag still flying the next morning.
tossups.r: That lawyer, Francis Scott Key, wrote the poem that became “The Star-Spangled Banner.” For 10 points, name this war that gave the United States its national anthem.

tossups.p: John Quincy Adams, Henry Clay, and Albert Gallatin were among the Americans who negotiated the treaty that ended this war in the city of Ghent, in what is now Belgium. That treaty, signed on Christmas Eve, returned both sides to the borders they had before the fighting.
tossups.r: Andrew Jackson’s victory at New Orleans came after that treaty was signed. For 10 points, name this war in which the British burned the White House.

clues.t: The United States vs. Great Britain, named for the year it began; nicknamed “America’s Second War of Independence”
Francis Scott Key wrote “The Star-Spangled Banner” after seeing the flag still flying over Fort McHenry in Baltimore (1814)
The British burned Washington, D.C., including the White House and the Capitol (1814); Dolley Madison had George Washington’s portrait saved
Andrew Jackson won the Battle of New Orleans (January 1815) after the peace treaty had already been signed
Ended by the Treaty of Ghent, signed on Christmas Eve 1814 by negotiators like John Quincy Adams and Henry Clay; borders went back to how they were
Oliver Hazard Perry won the Battle of Lake Erie (1813): “We have met the enemy and they are ours”; Americans then retook Detroit
Causes: British impressment (forcing American sailors into the Royal Navy) and British support for Native nations on the frontier
Shawnee leader Tecumseh, a British ally, was killed at the Battle of the Thames (1813) by William Henry Harrison’s army
“War Hawks” like Henry Clay and John C. Calhoun pushed Congress to declare war and hoped to conquer Canada
President James Madison asked Congress to declare war; Federalist critics called it “Mr. Madison’s War”
The USS _Constitution_ beat HMS _Guerriere_ and earned the nickname “Old Ironsides”
New England Federalists met at the Hartford Convention to protest the war; it helped destroy the Federalist Party
The British routed American militia at Bladensburg, Maryland, then marched into Washington (August 1814)
A storm with a tornado struck Washington during the British occupation, helping put out the fires
Lundy’s Lane, near Niagara Falls, was one of its bloodiest battles; Winfield Scott, whose gray-clad brigade had won at Chippawa, was wounded there
British general Isaac Brock took Detroit from William Hull, then was killed at Queenston Heights; Canadians honor him as a hero
At New Orleans, British general Edward Pakenham was killed attacking Jackson’s line on the Rodriguez Canal; Jean Lafitte’s pirates helped defend it
Macon’s Bill No. 2 (1810) tried to reopen trade; Napoleon tricked Madison into cutting off trade with Britain
Thomas Macdonough’s win on Lake Champlain at Plattsburgh (1814) turned back a British invasion from Canada
Americans burned government buildings in York (now Toronto), Upper Canada’s capital, in 1813; the British later cited it when burning Washington
Andrew Jackson defeated the Red Stick Creeks at Horseshoe Bend (1814); the Treaty of Fort Jackson took about 23 million acres
As he lay mortally wounded, Captain James Lawrence ordered “Don’t give up the ship”; those words went on Perry’s battle flag
Mary Pickersgill sewed the giant Fort McHenry flag, which is now at the Smithsonian

trap.title: Which war against Britain?
trap.body: The United States fought Great Britain twice in less than 40 years, and both wars have British invasions, battles near Canada, and famous flags, so players mix this war up with the American Revolution. Tchaikovsky’s _1812 Overture_, with its cannon blasts at Fourth of July concerts, is a different trap: it celebrates Russia’s defeat of Napoleon in 1812, not this war.
trap.fix: Revolution clues: Lexington and Concord, Saratoga, Valley Forge, Yorktown, and General George Washington. This war’s clues: impressment, the War Hawks, Lake Erie, the burning of Washington, Fort McHenry, the Hartford Convention, and Jackson at New Orleans. Say the whole name, “War of 1812,” because “1812” alone only earns a prompt.

topics.name: William Jennings Bryan
topics.kicker: Populist “Great Commoner” · Cross of Gold speech & Scopes Trial
topics.briefing: William Jennings Bryan was such a thrilling speaker that one speech, the 1896 “Cross of Gold,” won him the Democratic nomination for president when he was just 36. Farmers loved his call for “free silver,” but he lost all three of his presidential races. Later he served as Woodrow Wilson’s secretary of state and argued against Clarence Darrow in the 1925 Scopes Trial over teaching evolution.

sample.note: 10 real QBReader tossups (4 Middle School/Easy High School + 6 Regular High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: This man’s most popular talk on the Chautauqua [“shuh-TAW-kwuh”] lecture circuit, which brought speakers to small towns across America, was a religious speech called “The Prince of Peace.” He also published a newspaper named _The Commoner_, which echoed his own nickname.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this three-time Democratic presidential nominee who gave the “Cross of Gold” speech.

tossups.p: As a young congressman from Nebraska, this man fought for an income tax that was added to the Wilson-Gorman Tariff of 1894. Two years later, he called for coining unlimited silver at a ratio of sixteen to one with gold.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this “Great Commoner,” who lost the 1896 presidential election to William McKinley.

tossups.p: In one election, this man had two different running mates: the Democrats picked Arthur Sewall, while the Populists picked Thomas Watson. That same year, pro-gold “Gold Democrats” formed their own party to run against him.
tossups.r: He lost that 1896 race to William McKinley. For 10 points, name this champion of free silver.

tossups.p: While his opponent greeted visitors and gave speeches from his front porch in Ohio, this candidate crisscrossed the country by train, giving hundreds of speeches. His opponent’s campaign, run by Mark Hanna, raised far more money from big businesses.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this candidate who lost the 1896 election to William McKinley after giving the “Cross of Gold” speech.

tossups.p: Speaking up for farmers, this orator declared that “we have petitioned, and our petitions have been scorned,” and he warned that if farms were destroyed, “the grass will grow in the streets of every city in the country.”
tossups.r: That 1896 speech won him the Democratic nomination. For 10 points, name this man whose speech ended with the words “cross of gold.”

tossups.p: The character Matthew Harrison Brady in the play _Inherit the Wind_ is based on this man. In real life, this man helped prosecute a Tennessee teacher for teaching evolution, and defense lawyer Clarence Darrow questioned him about the Bible on the witness stand.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this three-time presidential candidate who also gave the “Cross of Gold” speech.

tossups.p: As secretary of state, this man signed a 1914 treaty with Nicaraguan diplomat Emiliano Chamorro [“chah-MOR-roh”] that gave the United States the right to build a canal through Nicaragua. He also signed “cooling-off” treaties in which nations promised to investigate disputes before going to war.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this secretary of state under Woodrow Wilson, famous for his “Cross of Gold” speech.

tossups.p: This official resigned from the cabinet in 1915 because he feared that the president’s stern notes to Germany after the sinking of the _Lusitania_ could drag the country into war. A lifelong non-drinker, he had served grape juice instead of wine to foreign diplomats.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this secretary of state under Woodrow Wilson, a three-time Democratic nominee for president.

tossups.p: At just 36 years old, this man became the youngest presidential nominee of a major party in American history. He won that nomination after a convention speech in Chicago that ended with him stretching out his arms as if on a cross.
tossups.r: Farmers cheered his call for free silver. For 10 points, name this orator of the “Cross of Gold” speech.

tossups.p: During the Spanish-American War, this man raised a regiment of Nebraska volunteers and served as its colonel, though his troops never reached the fighting. He is buried at Arlington National Cemetery.
tossups.r: In 1900 he made opposition to U.S. rule over the Philippines a major campaign issue. For 10 points, name this “Great Commoner.”

tossups.p: This speaker answered the supporters of the gold standard: “You shall not press down upon the brow of labor this crown of thorns.” He spoke for farmers and miners who wanted the government to coin silver freely so that more money would circulate.
tossups.r: He then won the 1896 Democratic nomination. For 10 points, name this man who gave the “Cross of Gold” speech.

tossups.p: In Dayton, Tennessee, this man took the witness stand as an expert on the Bible, and the defense lawyer questioned him about stories such as Jonah and the whale. He died in Dayton less than a week after the trial ended.
tossups.r: That 1925 trial was the Scopes Trial. For 10 points, name this three-time presidential nominee who opposed teaching evolution.

tossups.p: Born in Salem, Illinois, this man moved to Lincoln, Nebraska, where he won two terms in Congress in the early 1890s. He later edited the _Omaha World-Herald_ newspaper before running for president.
tossups.r: In 1896 the Populists joined the Democrats in nominating him. For 10 points, name this Nebraska politician nicknamed the “Great Commoner.”

tossups.p: This reformer supported the causes behind the 16th through 19th Amendments: an income tax, the direct election of senators, Prohibition, and women’s right to vote. Years earlier, he had argued that the gold standard hurt farmers and workers.
tossups.r: He lost his third race for president in 1908 to William Howard Taft. For 10 points, name this man who gave the “Cross of Gold” speech.

tossups.p: In his most famous speech, this man said the country needed “an Andrew Jackson” to stand up to organized wealth, and he argued that the money question mattered more than the tariff question. Delegates at the 1896 Democratic convention cheered wildly.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who said, “You shall not crucify mankind upon a cross of gold.”

clues.t: Gave the “Cross of Gold” speech at the 1896 Democratic convention in Chicago, which won him the nomination
Ran for president as the Democratic nominee three times (1896, 1900, 1908) and lost all three
Backed “free silver” and bimetallism: coining silver at a 16-to-1 ratio with gold, instead of a gold standard
Hero of farmers; in 1896 the Populist (People’s) Party joined the Democrats in nominating him
Nicknamed “the Great Commoner” for championing ordinary working people; from Nebraska
Helped prosecute a Tennessee teacher for teaching evolution in the 1925 Scopes Trial, facing defense lawyer Clarence Darrow
Woodrow Wilson’s first secretary of state; resigned in 1915 after the _Lusitania_ sinking, fearing Wilson’s stern protests would lead to war
Cross of Gold line: “You shall not press down upon the brow of labor this crown of thorns”
Lost twice to William McKinley (1896 and 1900), whose “front porch” campaign was run by Mark Hanna; lost in 1908 to William Howard Taft
At 36, the youngest presidential nominee of a major party in U.S. history (1896)
Broke tradition in 1896 by touring the country by train and giving hundreds of speeches in a whistle-stop campaign
A lifelong non-drinker who backed Prohibition; served grape juice instead of wine to diplomats
Made anti-imperialism his main issue in 1900, opposing U.S. rule over the Philippines
Other Cross of Gold lines: “destroy our farms and the grass will grow in the streets of every city” and a call for “an Andrew Jackson”
Published a newspaper called _The Commoner_ (from 1901); earlier edited the _Omaha World-Herald_
Star of the Chautauqua lecture circuit; his most famous talk was the religious speech “The Prince of Peace”
Had two 1896 running mates: Arthur Sewall (Democrats) and Thomas Watson (Populists)
Pro-gold “Gold Democrats” split off in 1896 to form the National Democratic Party against him
As a Nebraska congressman (1891–1895), pushed for the income tax in the Wilson-Gorman Tariff (1894)
As secretary of state, signed a 1914 treaty with Nicaragua’s Emiliano Chamorro giving the U.S. rights to build a canal there
Signed “cooling-off” treaties: nations agreed to let a commission investigate disputes before going to war
Darrow called him to the witness stand as a Bible expert and quizzed him about stories like Jonah and the whale
Died in Dayton, Tennessee, less than a week after the Scopes Trial ended (July 1925)
Colonel of a Nebraska volunteer regiment in the Spanish-American War (1898); buried at Arlington National Cemetery
The play _Inherit the Wind_ (1955) retells the Scopes Trial; its character Matthew Harrison Brady is based on him
Born in Salem, Illinois (1860); built his career in Lincoln, Nebraska

trap.title: Bryan, Darrow, or Scopes?
trap.body: The Scopes Trial shows up in tossups for several different answers. John Scopes was the Tennessee teacher on trial for teaching evolution, Clarence Darrow was his defense lawyer, and Bryan helped the prosecution, so a question asking for “this defense attorney” wants Darrow, not Bryan. On 1896 clues, don’t blurt out the winner, William McKinley, and don’t mix Bryan up with the poet William Cullen Bryant.
trap.fix: Bryan = the prosecution side, the Bible questions on the witness stand, free silver, the “Cross of Gold,” and resigning after the Lusitania sinking. Darrow = the defense, Scopes = the teacher, and McKinley = the man who beat Bryan twice. Plain “Bryan” is enough on real answer lines.

topics.name: Women’s Suffrage
topics.kicker: The fight to win women the vote · Won by the 19th Amendment in 1920
topics.briefing: For most of American history, women could not vote. Starting at the 1848 Seneca Falls Convention, activists like Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Susan B. Anthony, and later Alice Paul spent 72 years giving speeches, marching, picketing the White House, and even going to jail for the cause. In 1920 the 19th Amendment finally declared that the right to vote cannot be denied “on account of sex.”

qb.tip: All 8 are about women’s suffrage, but half of them open with British clues like Emily Davison and the Cat and Mouse Act, so learn the British side too.

sample.note: the 8 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: In _Minor v. Happersett_, the Supreme Court unanimously ruled that being a citizen did not automatically include this right, after a Missouri official refused to register Virginia Minor in 1872. Wyoming Territory had already granted this right to women in 1869.
tossups.r: Susan B. Anthony spent her life fighting for this cause. For 10 points, name this right that the 19th Amendment guaranteed to American women in 1920.

tossups.p: Judge Ward Hunt ordered a jury to find a woman guilty for exercising this right in Rochester, New York, in 1872, and she refused to pay her $100 fine. That woman had long worked with Elizabeth Cady Stanton to promote this cause.
tossups.r: That woman was Susan B. Anthony. For 10 points, name this cause, won nationally through the 19th Amendment, that gave women the ballot.

tossups.p: Protesters for this cause outraged crowds in 1917 by holding up banners that called the president “Kaiser Wilson.” Those protesters, known as the Silent Sentinels, were the first group ever to picket the White House.
tossups.r: They belonged to Alice Paul’s National Woman’s Party. For 10 points, name this cause that triumphed when the 19th Amendment was ratified in 1920.

tossups.p: Twenty-four-year-old Harry Burn switched his vote after his mother wrote urging him to “be a good boy,” making Tennessee the 36th state to approve an amendment for this cause in August 1920. Supporters of this cause wore yellow roses during that fight.
tossups.r: Carrie Chapman Catt led the final push. For 10 points, name this right guaranteed to women by the 19th Amendment.

tossups.p: William Bright introduced the 1869 bill that made Wyoming the first U.S. territory to grant this right to women. Wyoming insisted on keeping this right when it became a state in 1890, earning the nickname “the Equality State.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this right that Susan B. Anthony fought for, which the 19th Amendment extended to women nationwide.

tossups.p: The first complaint in one document says that man “has never permitted her to exercise her inalienable right to the elective franchise.” That document, signed by 68 women and 32 men, declared that “all men and women are created equal.”
tossups.r: That Declaration of Sentiments came from the 1848 Seneca Falls Convention. For 10 points, name this cause, the most debated demand at that convention.

tossups.p: Emily Davison died after she ran onto the track in front of King George V’s horse at the 1913 Epsom Derby during a protest for this cause. Her group, Emmeline Pankhurst’s WSPU, used the motto “Deeds, not words.”
tossups.r: In the United States, this cause won with the 19th Amendment. For 10 points, name this cause of the British suffragettes and Susan B. Anthony.

tossups.p: Britain’s “Cat and Mouse Act” of 1913 let jails release weakened hunger strikers who supported this cause, then arrest them again once they recovered. Some of those prisoners had been jailed for smashing shop windows in London.
tossups.r: Many British women over 30 won this right in 1918. For 10 points, name this right that American women gained through the 19th Amendment.

tossups.p: In 1893, New Zealand became the first self-governing country to grant this right to women, after Kate Sheppard organized huge petitions there. Switzerland did not grant this right in its national elections until 1971.
tossups.r: Susan B. Anthony led this cause in the United States. For 10 points, name this right guaranteed to American women by the 19th Amendment.

tossups.p: Inez Milholland rode a white horse at the front of a 1913 parade for this cause, held in Washington the day before Woodrow Wilson’s inauguration. During that march, Ida B. Wells refused to walk in a segregated section at the back and joined the Illinois marchers instead.
tossups.r: Alice Paul organized that parade. For 10 points, name this cause that won with the 19th Amendment.

tossups.p: In 1869, this movement split over whether to support the 15th Amendment, with Lucy Stone leading one group and Elizabeth Cady Stanton leading the other. The two groups reunited in 1890 to form NAWSA, which Carrie Chapman Catt later led.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this movement to win women the ballot, which finally succeeded with the 19th Amendment.

tossups.p: California senator Aaron Sargent first introduced a constitutional amendment for this cause in 1878, but it took more than 40 years to pass. That amendment was nicknamed for a woman who appeared on a dollar coin first minted in 1979.
tossups.r: That woman was Susan B. Anthony. For 10 points, name this cause, achieved when the 19th Amendment was ratified.

tossups.p: Montana’s Jeannette Rankin became the first woman elected to Congress in 1916, two years after her state granted this right. Like Montana, many western states adopted this right years before most eastern states did.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this right that became national for American women with the 19th Amendment in 1920.

tossups.p: In November 1917, guards at Virginia’s Occoquan Workhouse attacked jailed protesters for this cause during what became known as the “Night of Terror.” One of those protesters’ leaders went on a hunger strike in a Washington jail.
tossups.r: That leader, Alice Paul, headed the National Woman’s Party. For 10 points, name this cause achieved by the 19th Amendment.

tossups.p: Lucretia Mott met another reformer in London in 1840, after women were barred from taking part in the World Anti-Slavery Convention there. Eight years later, the two women organized a meeting in upstate New York that demanded this right and others.
tossups.r: That meeting was the Seneca Falls Convention. For 10 points, name this right, later championed by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony.

The Silent Sentinels picketed Woodrow Wilson’s White House (1917)
Alice Paul led the protest-minded National Woman’s Party and organized a huge 1913 parade in Washington
Carrie Chapman Catt led NAWSA’s “Winning Plan” and founded the League of Women Voters (1920)
Wyoming Territory was the first U.S. territory to let women vote (1869), and it kept that right as a state (1890)
Jailed activists in Britain and the U.S. went on hunger strikes
Britain: Emmeline Pankhurst’s WSPU (“Deeds, not words”) led the suffragettes; women over 30 won the vote in 1918, equal voting in 1928
_Minor v. Happersett_ (1875): the Supreme Court unanimously ruled that citizenship did not include the vote
Anthony was arrested for voting in 1872; Judge Ward Hunt told the jury to find her guilty, and she never paid her $100 fine
Picketers’ banners called the president “Kaiser Wilson” during World War I
Britain’s “Cat and Mouse Act” (1913) freed weak hunger strikers, then re-arrested them
Emily Davison died after running onto the track in front of King George V’s horse at the 1913 Epsom Derby
Tennessee became the 36th state to ratify (August 1920) when 24-year-old Harry Burn switched his vote after a letter from his mother
William Bright introduced Wyoming Territory’s 1869 law
The movement split in 1869 over the 15th Amendment (Stanton and Anthony vs. Lucy Stone); the groups merged as NAWSA in 1890
New Zealand was the first self-governing country to let women vote (1893, led by Kate Sheppard); Switzerland waited until 1971
At the 1913 parade, Inez Milholland rode a white horse, and Ida B. Wells refused to march in a segregated section
Senator Aaron Sargent first introduced the “Anthony Amendment” in 1878; Anthony later appeared on a 1979 dollar coin
Montana’s Jeannette Rankin became the first woman elected to Congress (1916)
The “Night of Terror” (November 1917): guards attacked jailed picketers at Virginia’s Occoquan Workhouse
Mott and Stanton met in London in 1840, when women were shut out of the World Anti-Slavery Convention

trap.title: Say “women”!
trap.body: “Suffrage” just means the right to vote, so real answer lines prompt on bare “suffrage” or “voting rights” and want you to say who got the vote. Players also blurt “15th Amendment,” which protected Black men’s votes in 1870 and split the movement, or “abolition,” since many suffragists started out as abolitionists. The 19th Amendment is how the right was won, not the name of the cause.
trap.fix: Answer “women’s suffrage” or “women’s right to vote.” Remember 15 = race (1870) and 19 = sex (1920). Say “19th Amendment” only if the question asks for “this amendment.”
trap.line: Real answer line: women’s suffrage (or women’s right to vote; accept similar answers about women voting; prompt on answers that do not mention women)

topics.briefing: Thomas Jefferson was only 33 when he wrote the first draft of the Declaration of Independence, with its famous words “all men are created equal,” yet he enslaved more than 600 people during his life. As the third president, he doubled the size of the country with the Louisiana Purchase and sent Lewis and Clark to explore it. He also designed his hilltop home, Monticello, which appears on the back of the nickel.

qb.tip: All five end with “third president,” so race the early clues; the “Ograbme” turtle cartoon (embargo spelled backward) is the favorite power clue.

sample.note: 9 real QBReader tossups (5 Middle School/Easy High School + 4 Regular High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: A political cartoon showed a snapping turtle named “Ograbme” [“oh-GRAB-mee”], which is “embargo” spelled backward, biting a smuggler who was carrying a barrel toward a ship. That cartoon mocked this president’s 1807 law that kept American ships from sailing to foreign ports.
tossups.r: This president had earlier bought the Louisiana Territory from France. For 10 points, name this third U.S. president.

tossups.p: While serving as the American minister to France, this diplomat wrote the artist Maria Cosway a famous letter in the form of a dialogue between his “Head” and his “Heart.” He came home to become the first U.S. Secretary of State.
tossups.r: In that job, he clashed with Alexander Hamilton over a national bank. For 10 points, name this author of the Declaration of Independence.

tossups.p: After the frigate USS _Philadelphia_ ran aground and was captured near Tripoli, Stephen Decatur led a nighttime raid to burn it so the enemy could not use it. This president had sent warships to the Mediterranean after the ruler of Tripoli demanded more tribute money.
tossups.r: U.S. Marines later fought at Derna [“DAIR-nuh”] in that First Barbary War. For 10 points, name this president who sent Lewis and Clark to explore the West.

tossups.p: The only full-length book this man published, _Notes on the State of Virginia_, began as answers to questions from the French diplomat François Barbé-Marbois [“bar-BAY mar-BWAH”]. More than twenty years later, Barbé-Marbois sold an enormous territory to this man’s negotiators, Robert Livingston and James Monroe.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who doubled the size of the United States with the Louisiana Purchase.

tossups.p: After British troops burned the Capitol in 1814, this retired president sold more than 6,000 of his books to Congress so it could rebuild its library. He spent his last years founding a university in Charlottesville and designing its domed Rotunda.
tossups.r: His home, Monticello, sits on a nearby mountaintop. For 10 points, name this third U.S. president.

tossups.p: This president refused to send the Monroe–Pinkney Treaty to the Senate because it did not end British impressment of American sailors. After the British warship _Leopard_ fired on the frigate _Chesapeake_ in 1807, he responded by stopping American ships from trading overseas.
tossups.r: That Embargo Act badly hurt merchants in New England. For 10 points, name this third U.S. president.

tossups.p: This man’s tombstone, which he designed himself, calls him the author of the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom and the father of a university, but it never mentions his presidency. James Madison got that statute passed in 1786 while this man was serving as a diplomat in France.
tossups.r: He died on July 4, 1826, exactly fifty years after the Declaration of Independence was adopted. For 10 points, name this third U.S. president.

tossups.p: In one election, this candidate tied his own running mate, Aaron Burr, in the Electoral College, so the House of Representatives had to vote 36 times to pick the winner. To prevent another tie like that, the states ratified the Twelfth Amendment.
tossups.r: This man later called his win the “Revolution of 1800.” For 10 points, name this Democratic-Republican who defeated John Adams to become the third president.

tossups.p: In the first presidential inauguration held in Washington, D.C., this man tried to calm a divided country by declaring, “We are all Republicans, we are all Federalists.” His Secretary of State, James Madison, was sued in the Supreme Court case _Marbury v. Madison_.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who sent Lewis and Clark to explore the lands he bought from France.

tossups.p: While he was vice president, this man secretly wrote the Kentucky Resolutions, which argued that states could declare federal laws unconstitutional. His close friend James Madison wrote a similar set of resolutions for Virginia, and both protested the Alien and Sedition Acts.
tossups.r: As president, he pardoned people convicted under the Sedition Act. For 10 points, name this man who defeated John Adams in the election of 1800.

tossups.p: Using a razor and glue, this thinker cut verses from the Gospels to create _The Life and Morals of Jesus of Nazareth_, a book that kept Jesus’s moral teachings but left out the miracles. He was proud of writing a Virginia law that guaranteed freedom of religion.
tossups.r: This owner of Monticello also bought the Louisiana Territory from France. For 10 points, name this third U.S. president.

tossups.p: Congress deleted a long passage in this delegate’s draft that blamed King George III for the slave trade. John Adams later recalled telling this younger Virginian, “You can write ten times better than I can,” when the Committee of Five chose him to write that draft.
tossups.r: That document was adopted on July 4, 1776. For 10 points, name this Virginian who wrote the Declaration of Independence.

tossups.p: When people in France asked if he was the man replacing Benjamin Franklin, this American minister usually answered, “No one can replace him, Sir; I am only his successor.” In Paris, he had his enslaved cook, James Hemings, trained as a French chef.
tossups.r: James’s sister Sally Hemings was among the more than 600 people this man enslaved during his life. For 10 points, name this owner of Monticello and third U.S. president.

tossups.p: In an 1802 letter to a group of Baptists in Danbury, Connecticut, this president wrote that the First Amendment built a “wall of separation between church and state.” As vice president, he had secretly written the Kentucky Resolutions against the Alien and Sedition Acts.
tossups.r: He sent Lewis and Clark to explore the West. For 10 points, name this president who bought the Louisiana Territory from Napoleon.

tossups.p: After years of political anger, this man and an old rival from Massachusetts became pen pals again when Benjamin Rush encouraged them to make peace. This man died at his Virginia home on July 4, 1826, just hours before that rival died.
tossups.r: That rival was John Adams. For 10 points, name this third U.S. president, the main author of the Declaration of Independence.

Secretly wrote the Kentucky Resolutions against the Alien and Sedition Acts (Madison wrote Virginia’s)
Won the election of 1800 after an Electoral College tie with Aaron Burr, who became his vice president; the tie led to the 12th Amendment
Died July 4, 1826, the Declaration’s 50th anniversary, a few hours before John Adams
A cartoon snapping turtle named “Ograbme” (embargo spelled backward) mocked his Embargo Act
First Barbary War against Tripoli: Stephen Decatur burned the captured USS _Philadelphia_ (1804); Marines fought at Derna (1805)
Wrote the artist Maria Cosway a letter set up as a dialogue between “My Head and My Heart”
Minister to France (1785–1789) after Benjamin Franklin; his enslaved cook James Hemings trained as a chef in Paris
Wrote _Notes on the State of Virginia_, his only full-length book, answering questions from François Barbé-Marbois

Founded the University of Virginia in Charlottesville and designed its buildings, including the domed Rotunda
Wrote the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom; his tombstone lists it, the Declaration, and the university, but not the presidency

trap.title: Jefferson or Madison?
trap.body: Thomas Jefferson and James Madison were lifelong partners. They founded the Democratic-Republican Party together and secretly wrote the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions (Jefferson wrote Kentucky’s, Madison wrote Virginia’s), and Madison was Jefferson’s Secretary of State before becoming the next president. A clue like “his Secretary of State was sued in _Marbury v. Madison_” is about Jefferson, so buzzing “Madison” because you heard the name loses the tossup.
trap.fix: Jefferson clues: the Declaration, the Louisiana Purchase, Lewis and Clark, the Embargo Act, Monticello, and the University of Virginia. Madison clues: “Father of the Constitution,” the Bill of Rights, _The Federalist Papers_, the War of 1812, and his home, Montpelier. And never answer Jefferson for Jefferson Davis, the president of the Confederacy.

topics.name: Trail of Tears
topics.kicker: Forced removal of Native nations west · Result of the Indian Removal Act
topics.briefing: In 1838, U.S. soldiers forced about 16,000 Cherokee people out of their homes in Georgia and nearby states and sent them hundreds of miles west to Indian Territory, in what is now Oklahoma. Thousands died of disease, hunger, and cold in crowded camps and on the journey. The Choctaw, Creek, Chickasaw, and Seminole nations were forced west too, all under the Indian Removal Act that Andrew Jackson signed in 1830.

qb.tip: Only 2 results at this level, so add Regular High School; one of those wants “Indian removal” (the policy), and one old novice question wrongly says the Supreme Court ruled against the Cherokee, when Worcester v. Georgia actually sided with them.

sample.note: 5 real QBReader tossups (2 Middle School/Easy High School + 3 Regular High School, power-marked; 1 of them wanted “Indian removal”)

tossups.p: An 1829 gold rush near Dahlonega [“duh-LON-uh-guh”], Georgia, made settlers even more eager to take the land of the people forced into this event. Their Principal Chief, John Ross, later convinced General Winfield Scott to let them lead most of this journey themselves.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this forced removal of the Cherokee and other Native nations to what is now Oklahoma.

tossups.p: A small Treaty Party led by Major Ridge and Elias Boudinot [“BOO-dih-noh”] signed away Cherokee land at New Echota [“eh-CHOH-tuh”] in 1835, and the U.S. used that treaty to justify this event. Principal Chief John Ross and most Cherokees rejected the treaty.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this forced march of the Cherokee to Indian Territory in 1838 and 1839.

tossups.p: The Supreme Court ruled in _Worcester v. Georgia_ that Georgia’s laws had no force inside the Cherokee Nation, but the ruling failed to prevent this event. Andrew Jackson supposedly answered, “John Marshall has made his decision; now let him enforce it.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this forced removal of the Cherokee and other nations to land west of the Mississippi River.

tossups.p: Tennessee congressman Davy Crockett broke with President Andrew Jackson by voting against the 1830 law that led to this event. That law let the president trade land in the West for the homelands of Native nations in the East.
tossups.r: That law was the Indian Removal Act. For 10 points, name this forced march of thousands of Cherokee to present-day Oklahoma.

tossups.p: The Choctaw leader George W. Harkins wrote a “Farewell Letter to the American People” as his nation began this event under the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek. The Choctaw were the first of five Southeastern nations forced west in this event.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this series of forced removals of Native Americans, most famously the Cherokee, to Indian Territory in the 1830s.

tossups.p: Seminoles who rejected the Treaty of Payne’s Landing attacked Major Francis Dade’s soldiers in 1835, starting a long war to avoid this event. Osceola [“oss-ee-OH-luh”] led Seminole resistance in Florida until he was captured under a flag of truce.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this forced removal of Native Americans that the Cherokee remember as “the trail where they cried.”

tossups.p: Ralph Waldo Emerson wrote a public letter to President Martin Van Buren in 1838 begging him to stop this event. That year, soldiers under General Winfield Scott forced thousands of people out of their homes and into crowded stockades.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this forced march of the Cherokee people west to Indian Territory.

tossups.p: In the case _Cherokee Nation v. Georgia_, John Marshall described the main victims of this event as one of the “domestic dependent nations.” Their Principal Chief, John Ross, fought this event for years with lawsuits and petitions to Congress.
tossups.r: It followed the Indian Removal Act of 1830. For 10 points, name this forced removal of the Cherokee to present-day Oklahoma.

tossups.p: Survivors of this event made Tahlequah [“TAL-uh-kwah”] their nation’s new capital in 1839. During this event, many groups were stuck for weeks in the winter of 1838 to 1839, waiting to cross icy rivers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this forced march of thousands of Cherokee from the Southeast to Indian Territory.

tossups.p: Some Cherokees avoided this event by staying in the mountains of North Carolina, and their descendants make up the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians. Thousands of people died of disease, hunger, and cold during this event.
tossups.r: President Andrew Jackson’s Indian Removal Act led to this event. For 10 points, name this forced march to present-day Oklahoma.

tossups.p: This event forced the Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, and Seminole, along with one other nation, out of their homelands in the American Southeast. White Americans called those nations the “Five Civilized Tribes” because they had adopted some American customs.
tossups.r: The fifth nation was the Cherokee. For 10 points, name this forced relocation to Indian Territory in the 1830s.

tossups.p: Before this event, its best-known victims had written a constitution and printed the _Cherokee Phoenix_, a newspaper that used Sequoyah’s [“sih-KWOY-uh”] writing system. None of that stopped Georgia from taking their land.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this forced march of the Cherokee people to Indian Territory after the Indian Removal Act.

tossups.p: In 1987, Congress honored the victims of this event by creating a historic route, now marked by the National Park Service across nine states. Some groups in this event traveled by boat, but most went over land, and many did not arrive in the West until early 1839.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this forced removal of the Cherokee from the Southeast to Indian Territory.

tossups.p: Although the law that led to this event was signed by the previous president, most of the Cherokee were removed while Martin Van Buren was president. About 16,000 Cherokee people were forced to leave their homes in this event.
tossups.r: Andrew Jackson had signed the Indian Removal Act in 1830. For 10 points, name this deadly forced march to present-day Oklahoma.

tossups.p: Georgia held lotteries that gave away land belonging to the main victims of this event, including an 1832 lottery for land and gold lots. The missionary Samuel Worcester was jailed for living among those victims without a license from Georgia.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this forced removal of the Cherokee people to Indian Territory in 1838 and 1839.

clues.t: The forced removal of Native American nations from the Southeast to land west of the Mississippi River in the 1830s
Followed the Indian Removal Act, signed by President Andrew Jackson in 1830
Ended in Indian Territory, which is now the state of Oklahoma
Best known for the Cherokee removal of 1838–1839, when thousands of Cherokee people died
The “Five Civilized Tribes” were all forced west: the Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek (Muscogee), and Seminole
_Worcester v. Georgia_ (1832): John Marshall’s Supreme Court sided with the Cherokee, but Georgia and Jackson ignored the ruling
Treaty of New Echota (1835): a small group of Cherokees signed away their nation’s land without its approval
Principal Chief John Ross fought removal with lawsuits and petitions, then led many of the groups west
The Cherokee remember it as “the trail where they cried”
The Seminoles of Florida fought the Second Seminole War to avoid removal; Osceola was a famous leader
Most Cherokees were forced west in 1838–1839, under President Martin Van Buren
General Winfield Scott’s soldiers forced the Cherokee into stockades in 1838 before the march
Seminoles who rejected the Treaty of Payne’s Landing (1832) began the Second Seminole War by attacking Major Dade’s troops (1835)
The Choctaw went first, under the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek (1830); George W. Harkins wrote a “Farewell Letter to the American People”
An 1829 gold rush near Dahlonega, Georgia, made settlers want Cherokee land even more
Congressman Davy Crockett of Tennessee voted against the Indian Removal Act
Major Ridge and Elias Boudinot led the Treaty Party that signed the Treaty of New Echota
_Cherokee Nation v. Georgia_ (1831): John Marshall called Native peoples “domestic dependent nations”
Ralph Waldo Emerson wrote a public letter to President Van Buren in 1838 protesting the Cherokee removal
Before removal, the Cherokee had a written constitution (1827) and a newspaper, the _Cherokee Phoenix_, printed partly in Sequoyah’s writing system
Georgia gave away Cherokee land in lotteries, including an 1832 land and gold lottery; missionary Samuel Worcester was jailed for living among the Cherokee
In the winter of 1838–1839, many groups were stuck for weeks waiting to cross icy rivers
Survivors made Tahlequah, Oklahoma, the Cherokee Nation’s capital in 1839
Some Cherokees stayed in the North Carolina mountains; their descendants are the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians

trap.title: Law, Policy, or March?
trap.body: Three answers sound alike. The Indian Removal Act is the 1830 law Andrew Jackson signed, “Indian removal” is the whole policy, and the Trail of Tears is the deadly forced march, especially the Cherokee removal of 1838–1839. Real answer lines prompt on “Indian Removal Act,” and one real tossup wanted “Indian removal” and took “Trail of Tears” only before those words were read. The Long Walk of the Navajo (1864) was a different forced march, in the Southwest.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this law” or “this act” wants the Indian Removal Act, “this policy” wants Indian removal, and “this event,” “this march,” or “this journey” wants the Trail of Tears. If you get a prompt, say “Trail of Tears.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Trail of Tears (prompt on Indian Removal or the Indian Removal Act until mentioned; prompt on descriptions such as “removal of Native Americans”)

topics.name: Woodrow Wilson
topics.kicker: 28th U.S. President · World War I & the Fourteen Points
topics.briefing: Woodrow Wilson is the only president who earned a PhD, and he ran Princeton University before becoming the 28th president. He won reelection in 1916 with the slogan “He kept us out of war,” then led the United States into World War I just a few months later. His Fourteen Points called for a League of Nations, but the Senate refused to approve the peace treaty, so America never joined.

sample.note: 4 real QBReader tossups (1 Middle School/Easy High School + 3 Regular High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: During this president’s first term, the Keating-Owen Act tried to stop factories from shipping goods made by child labor, but the Supreme Court struck it down in 1918. This president also signed the Adamson Act, which gave railroad workers an eight-hour day.
tossups.r: He won a second term in 1916 with the slogan “He kept us out of war.” For 10 points, name this 28th president.

tossups.p: To build support for a war, this president created the Committee on Public Information, whose “Four Minute Men” gave short patriotic speeches in movie theaters. He also signed the Espionage Act, under which the socialist Eugene Debs was later jailed for an antiwar speech.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who led the United States into World War I.

tossups.p: This president learned of a secret telegram from German official Arthur Zimmermann that offered to help Mexico win back Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona. Weeks later, he asked Congress to declare war, saying “the world must be made safe for democracy.”
tossups.r: His Fourteen Points later laid out a plan for peace. For 10 points, name this president during World War I.

tossups.p: After a German submarine sank the British liner _Lusitania_ in 1915, killing more than 100 Americans, this president sent protests so strong that his secretary of state, William Jennings Bryan, resigned.
tossups.r: In 1917, after Germany restarted unrestricted submarine warfare, he asked Congress to declare war. For 10 points, name this 28th president.

tossups.p: This president’s Treasury secretary, William McAdoo, helped set up a new system of twelve regional banks to manage the nation’s money. That system, the Federal Reserve, was part of this president’s New Freedom program, which also lowered tariffs.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Democrat who was president during World War I.

tossups.p: Senator Henry Cabot Lodge demanded changes, called “reservations,” before he would support a treaty this president had helped write. This president refused to compromise, and the Senate rejected that treaty, which kept the United States out of the League of Nations.
tossups.r: He still won the Nobel Peace Prize for his work on the League. For 10 points, name this president who proposed the Fourteen Points.

tossups.p: Near the end of this president’s second term, his attorney general, A. Mitchell Palmer, had thousands of suspected radicals arrested during the First Red Scare. Years earlier, this president had signed the Clayton Antitrust Act, which protected labor unions.
tossups.r: He also proposed a League of Nations. For 10 points, name this president who led the U.S. through World War I.

tossups.p: Colonel Edward House, this president’s closest adviser, organized a team of experts called “The Inquiry” to plan the world after a great war. Their work helped shape a January 1918 speech in which this president called for an independent Poland and freedom of the seas.
tossups.r: That speech listed his Fourteen Points for peace. For 10 points, name this president who led the U.S. into World War I.

tossups.p: After Pancho Villa’s men raided Columbus, New Mexico, in 1916, this president sent General John J. Pershing into Mexico to chase Villa. Two years earlier, he had ordered U.S. troops to occupy the Mexican port of Veracruz [“vair-uh-KROOZ”].
tossups.r: Pershing later led American troops in World War I. For 10 points, name this president who led the U.S. into that war.

tossups.p: Before entering politics, this man earned a PhD from Johns Hopkins, the only president with that degree, and he served as president of Princeton University. He then won election as governor of New Jersey in 1910.
tossups.r: Two years later, he won the White House when Theodore Roosevelt and William Howard Taft split the Republican vote. For 10 points, name this Democrat.

tossups.p: This leader became the first sitting American president to visit Europe when he sailed to the Paris Peace Conference in 1918. There, he joined David Lloyd George, Georges Clemenceau [“KLEM-un-soh”], and Vittorio Orlando as one of the “Big Four.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this American president who hoped a League of Nations would prevent future wars.

tossups.p: While touring the country by train to win support for the League of Nations, this president collapsed in Pueblo, Colorado. After his stroke in 1919, his wife Edith screened his papers and visitors, and he later forced out Secretary of State Robert Lansing for holding cabinet meetings without him.
tossups.r: This Democrat had led the nation through World War I. For 10 points, name this 28th president.

tossups.p: In 1917, Alice Paul’s “Silent Sentinels” stood outside this president’s White House with banners asking how long women must wait for liberty. He eventually supported the 19th Amendment, which gave women the right to vote in 1920.
tossups.r: He vetoed the Volstead Act, which enforced Prohibition, but Congress overrode him. For 10 points, name this president during World War I.

tossups.p: This president’s administration segregated many federal offices, a racist policy that hurt Black government workers. In 1915 he showed the racist film _The Birth of a Nation_ at the White House.
tossups.r: He had grown up in the South during the Civil War. For 10 points, name this Democrat who led the U.S. into World War I.

tossups.p: In 1913, this president became the first since John Adams to speak to Congress in person, asking it to lower tariffs. That request led to the Underwood Tariff, and he also created the Federal Trade Commission to police unfair business practices.
tossups.r: He later won the 1919 Nobel Peace Prize. For 10 points, name this president whose reform program was called the New Freedom.

The Fourteen Points (January 1918): his plan for a fair peace after World War I
28th President (1913–1921), a Democrat who served two terms
Championed the League of Nations, but the Senate rejected the Treaty of Versailles, so the U.S. never joined
Won reelection in 1916 with the slogan “He kept us out of war”
A German submarine sank the _Lusitania_ (1915); his strong protests led Secretary of State William Jennings Bryan to resign
The Zimmermann Telegram (1917): Germany secretly offered to help Mexico win back Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona

His reform program, the New Freedom, cut tariffs with the Underwood Tariff (1913) and created the Federal Trade Commission (1914)
The only president with a PhD; he led Princeton University (1902–1910) and was governor of New Jersey (1911–1913)
Won the 1912 election when the Republicans split between William Howard Taft and Theodore Roosevelt’s Bull Moose Party
Collapsed in Pueblo, Colorado, on a 1919 tour for the League; after his stroke, his wife Edith screened his papers and visitors
Won the 1919 Nobel Peace Prize for his work creating the League of Nations
Alice Paul’s “Silent Sentinels” picketed his White House (1917); he later backed the 19th Amendment, which gave women the vote (1920)
Signed the Clayton Antitrust Act (1914), which banned unfair practices like price discrimination and protected labor unions
The Keating-Owen Act (1916) barred goods made by child labor from interstate trade; the Supreme Court struck it down in 1918
The Adamson Act (1916) gave railroad workers an eight-hour day and headed off a national rail strike
The Palmer Raids (1919–1920): his attorney general, A. Mitchell Palmer, had thousands of suspected radicals arrested in the First Red Scare
His Committee on Public Information (led by George Creel) sent “Four Minute Men” to give short speeches supporting the war
Colonel Edward House, his closest adviser, organized “The Inquiry,” a team of experts that helped plan the Fourteen Points
Senator Henry Cabot Lodge (with his “reservations”) and the “Irreconcilables” led the Senate fight against the Treaty of Versailles
The Fourteen Points called for open diplomacy, freedom of the seas, self-determination for peoples, and an independent Poland
Forced out Secretary of State Robert Lansing (1920) for holding cabinet meetings while he was sick
Sent General John J. Pershing into Mexico (1916) to chase Pancho Villa after Villa’s raid on Columbus, New Mexico
His administration segregated many federal offices, a racist policy that hurt Black government workers
First sitting president to visit Europe; one of the “Big Four” at the Paris Peace Conference (1919) with Lloyd George, Clemenceau, and Orlando
Signed the Espionage Act (1917) and Sedition Act (1918); the socialist Eugene Debs was jailed for an antiwar speech
Vetoed the Volstead Act (1919), which enforced Prohibition, but Congress overrode the veto

trap.title: President or his plan?
trap.body: Quiz bowl also has tossups whose answer is the Fourteen Points, the League of Nations, or the Treaty of Versailles, and they use many of the same clues as this one. If the question says “this speech,” “this organization,” or “this treaty,” answering “Wilson” is wrong, and an early wrong buzz costs 5 points. His New Freedom reforms can also sound like Theodore Roosevelt’s Square Deal.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this president” or “this man” means Wilson. Then sort the reforms: the Clayton Antitrust Act, the Federal Reserve, and the New Freedom are Wilson, while the Square Deal and the Rough Riders are Theodore Roosevelt. Plain “Wilson” is enough on real answer lines.

topics.name: Alexander Hamilton
topics.kicker: 1st Secretary of the Treasury · Built the nation’s money system
topics.briefing: Alexander Hamilton was born on the tiny Caribbean island of Nevis, lost his mother as a boy, and wrote his way to the American colonies, where he became George Washington’s right-hand man in the Revolution. As the first Secretary of the Treasury, he built the young nation’s money system, and his face is on the $10 bill. He was killed in an 1804 duel with Aaron Burr, and his life story became the hit musical _Hamilton_.

sample.note: 13 real QBReader tossups (6 Middle School/Easy High School + 7 Regular High School, power-marked; 1 asked for the Burr–Hamilton duel)

tossups.p: While studying at King’s College, now Columbia University, this young man spoke to an angry Patriot mob on the college steps so that its Loyalist president, Myles Cooper, could escape. During the Revolution, he became an aide-de-camp to George Washington.
tossups.r: He later served as the first Secretary of the Treasury. For 10 points, name this Founding Father who was killed in a duel by Aaron Burr.

tossups.p: As a college student, this writer answered the Loyalist minister Samuel Seabury with the pamphlets _A Full Vindication of the Measures of Congress_ and _The Farmer Refuted_. Years later, he joined James Madison and John Jay in writing essays under the pen name “Publius.”
tossups.r: Those essays, _The Federalist Papers_, defended the Constitution. For 10 points, name this first Secretary of the Treasury.

tossups.p: At the Battle of Yorktown, this officer led a nighttime bayonet charge that captured Redoubt No. 10 from the British. He had spent four years before that as one of George Washington’s most trusted aides-de-camp.
tossups.r: During the war he married Elizabeth Schuyler, a general’s daughter. For 10 points, name this New Yorker who became the first Secretary of the Treasury.

tossups.p: With Egbert Benson, this delegate represented New York at the 1786 Annapolis Convention, where he wrote the report calling for a bigger meeting in Philadelphia the next year. At that Philadelphia meeting, he was the only New York delegate to sign the new Constitution.
tossups.r: He then wrote most of _The Federalist Papers_ to defend it. For 10 points, name this first Secretary of the Treasury.

tossups.p: In one essay, this author argued that “energy in the executive” is a key part of good government. In another, he called the courts the “least dangerous” branch because they control neither the sword nor the purse. He wrote 51 of the 85 essays in that series.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this main author of _The Federalist Papers_, who later became the first Secretary of the Treasury.

tossups.p: The U.S. Coast Guard traces its history to the Revenue Cutter Service, a fleet of small armed ships this official created in 1790 to stop smugglers from dodging taxes. This official also paid for the new government by taxing whiskey.
tossups.r: That tax sparked the Whiskey Rebellion. For 10 points, name this first Secretary of the Treasury, who appears on the $10 bill.

tossups.p: When the speculator William Duer’s collapse helped cause the Panic of 1792, this official used a “sinking fund” to buy government bonds and calm the markets. That fund had been part of his plan to pay off the debts from the Revolution.
tossups.r: His Report on Public Credit called for the national government to take over the states’ war debts. For 10 points, name this first Secretary of the Treasury.

tossups.p: At a 1790 dinner hosted by Thomas Jefferson, this man and James Madison struck a famous bargain: Southern votes for his debt plan in exchange for putting the new national capital on the Potomac River. That deal is called the Compromise of 1790.
tossups.r: A rap “Cabinet Battle” in a 2015 Broadway musical shows him fighting with Jefferson over that debt plan. For 10 points, name this first Secretary of the Treasury.

tossups.p: This official’s Report on Manufactures argued that tariffs and cash “bounties” could help young American factories compete with Britain’s. Congress did not adopt most of that 1791 report, but his plan for a national bank passed the same year.
tossups.r: He argued with Thomas Jefferson over whether that First Bank of the United States was constitutional. For 10 points, name this first Secretary of the Treasury.

tossups.p: When President Washington asked his cabinet whether a national bank was constitutional, this official argued that the “necessary and proper” clause gave Congress implied powers to create one. Washington agreed and signed the bank bill in 1791.
tossups.r: Thomas Jefferson had argued the opposite. For 10 points, name this first Secretary of the Treasury, who created the First Bank of the United States.

tossups.p: After James Reynolds blackmailed him, this official published a 1797 pamphlet confessing to a personal scandal involving Reynolds’s wife, Maria. He made the scandal public to prove that the secret payments were not stolen Treasury money, but the confession badly damaged his reputation.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this first Secretary of the Treasury, who was later killed in a duel with Aaron Burr.

tossups.p: This man nearly fought a duel with James Monroe in 1797, blaming Monroe for leaking papers about one of his scandals; Aaron Burr helped calm the dispute. In the tied election of 1800, this man urged Federalists in the House to choose Thomas Jefferson over Burr.
tossups.r: Burr killed him in a duel four years later. For 10 points, name this first Secretary of the Treasury.

tossups.p: During the Quasi-War with France, this former cabinet member was made a major general and second-in-command of a new army, under the aging George Washington. Two years later, he wrote a pamphlet attacking President John Adams, which split their Federalist Party.
tossups.r: He was later killed in a duel by Aaron Burr. For 10 points, name this Federalist leader and first Secretary of the Treasury.

tossups.p: A newspaper printed Dr. Charles Cooper’s letter claiming that this man had expressed a “despicable opinion” of a rival who had just lost the 1804 race for governor of New York. That rival demanded an explanation, and when this man would not give one, the two met at Weehawken, New Jersey.
tossups.r: That rival, Vice President Aaron Burr, shot this man in their duel. For 10 points, name this first Secretary of the Treasury.

tossups.p: After a hurricane struck St. Croix in 1772, this teenage clerk wrote a vivid letter about the storm that was printed in a local newspaper. Impressed readers raised money to send him to school in North America, far from his birthplace on the island of Nevis.
tossups.r: His life story became a hit 2015 musical by Lin-Manuel Miranda. For 10 points, name this first Secretary of the Treasury.

clues.t: First Secretary of the Treasury (1789–1795), under George Washington
Killed in an 1804 duel by Vice President Aaron Burr
Wrote 51 of the 85 essays in _The Federalist Papers_ with James Madison and John Jay, all signed “Publius”
His portrait is on the $10 bill
Title character of Lin-Manuel Miranda’s 2015 musical, with songs like “My Shot” and “Cabinet Battle”
Report on Public Credit (1790): the national government should assume (take over) the states’ Revolutionary War debts
Created the First Bank of the United States (1791), defending it with “implied powers”; Jefferson called it unconstitutional
Report on Manufactures (1791): tariffs and cash “bounties” to help American factories grow
His tax on whiskey led to the Whiskey Rebellion (1794) in western Pennsylvania
The duel was at Weehawken, New Jersey, across the Hudson River from New York City; his shot hit a tree branch above Burr
In the tied election of 1800, urged Federalists in the House to pick Thomas Jefferson over Aaron Burr
Born on Nevis in the West Indies and orphaned young; his letter about a 1772 hurricane on St. Croix got him sent to school in America
George Washington’s aide-de-camp in the Revolution; led a nighttime attack on Redoubt No. 10 at Yorktown (1781)
The Reynolds Pamphlet (1797): after James Reynolds blackmailed him, he confessed a personal scandal with Maria Reynolds to prove he never stole Treasury money
Compromise of 1790: at a dinner with Jefferson and Madison, the South backed his debt plan and the capital went on the Potomac River
With Egbert Benson, went to the Annapolis Convention (1786) and wrote its call for a Constitutional Convention; the only New York delegate to sign the Constitution
Used a “sinking fund” to calm the Panic of 1792, set off partly by the speculator William Duer
Founded the Revenue Cutter Service (1790), which grew into the U.S. Coast Guard
As a college student, answered Loyalist Samuel Seabury with _A Full Vindication_ and _The Farmer Refuted_
Talked to an angry mob so Myles Cooper, the Loyalist president of King’s College (now Columbia), could escape (1775)
Major general and second-in-command of the army in the Quasi-War with France; his 1800 pamphlet attacking John Adams split the Federalists
_Federalist_ No. 70 praises “energy in the executive”; No. 78 calls the courts the “least dangerous” branch
Nearly dueled James Monroe in 1797 over leaked scandal papers; Aaron Burr helped calm it down
Dr. Charles Cooper’s letter reported his “despicable opinion” of Burr after Burr lost the 1804 New York governor’s race
Married Elizabeth (Eliza) Schuyler; Burr had beaten her father, Philip Schuyler, for a U.S. Senate seat (1791)

trap.title: Hamilton or Burr?
trap.body: The 1804 duel at Weehawken is a stock clue for both men, and one of the six real results asks for the duel itself. Clues like the tied election of 1800, Philip Schuyler, and the 1804 New York governor’s race also fit Aaron Burr. If you buzz on “Weehawken” without hearing who died, you can lose the tossup.
trap.fix: Hamilton is the one who was killed: the first Treasury Secretary, the $10 bill, and most of _The Federalist Papers_. Burr fired the fatal shot: he was Thomas Jefferson’s vice president and was later tried for treason. If the question asks “in what event,” answer “the Burr–Hamilton duel.”

topics.kicker: Scottish-born steel tycoon · Gave his fortune away to build libraries
topics.briefing: Andrew Carnegie came to Pittsburgh from Scotland at age 12 and started out as a bobbin boy in a cotton mill, earning about a dollar a week. By 1901, when he sold his steel company to J.P. Morgan for about $480 million, he was one of the richest people on Earth. Then he gave most of it away, paying for more than 2,500 public libraries and a famous concert hall in New York.

sample.note: 8 real QBReader tossups (2 Middle School/Easy High School + 6 Regular High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: This man’s Keystone Bridge Company built James Eads’s bridge across the Mississippi River at St. Louis, which opened in 1874. Years earlier, he had made his first big profits by investing in a company that built railroad sleeping cars.
tossups.r: He sold his steel company to J.P. Morgan in 1901. For 10 points, name this Scottish-born steel tycoon who later gave away most of his fortune.

tossups.p: An essay by this man opens by calling “the proper administration of wealth” the “problem of our age.” That essay argues that rich people should give away their fortunes during their own lifetimes to help the public.
tossups.r: That essay is _The Gospel of Wealth_. For 10 points, name this steel tycoon who paid for more than 2,500 public libraries.

tossups.p: As a teenager, this man became the secretary and telegraph operator of Thomas A. Scott at the Pennsylvania Railroad. When the Civil War began, he helped Scott organize the Union’s military railroads and telegraph lines.
tossups.r: He later made his fortune in Pittsburgh’s steel mills. For 10 points, name this Scottish-born industrialist who wrote _The Gospel of Wealth_.

tossups.p: This man was in Scotland in 1892 when his partner Henry Clay Frick hired Pinkerton guards to break a strike at one of his steel plants. The battle that followed left several workers and guards dead, and state troops took over the town.
tossups.r: That fight was the Homestead Strike. For 10 points, name this Pittsburgh steel tycoon and philanthropist.

tossups.p: Charles M. Schwab helped negotiate the 1901 sale of this man’s company for about 480 million dollars. The buyer combined that company with several others to create U.S. Steel, the first billion-dollar corporation in history.
tossups.r: The buyer was J.P. Morgan. For 10 points, name this Scottish-born steel tycoon who spent his last years giving his money away.

tossups.p: This man offered 20 million dollars, the same amount the United States had paid Spain, so that the Philippines could buy its independence. He also founded the Church Peace Union and paid for the Peace Palace in The Hague.
tossups.r: He wrote _The Gospel of Wealth_. For 10 points, name this steel tycoon and philanthropist.

tossups.p: After the 1889 Johnstown Flood, this member of the club that owned the failed South Fork Dam paid to give Johnstown a new library. Towns that accepted his library gifts had to provide the land and pay for the upkeep.
tossups.r: He funded more than 2,500 public libraries in all. For 10 points, name this steel tycoon and philanthropist.

tossups.p: A _Diplodocus_ skeleton nicknamed “Dippy” was dug up by an expedition from this man’s museum, and its species was named in his honor. He sent copies of that skeleton to museums in London, Paris, and other cities.
tossups.r: His partner Henry Clay Frick broke the 1892 Homestead Strike at one of his plants. For 10 points, name this Pittsburgh steel tycoon.

tossups.p: After rescuers died in a 1904 coal mine disaster near Pittsburgh, this man created a Hero Fund to honor people who risk their lives to save others. In 1910, he founded an Endowment for International Peace.
tossups.r: He believed rich people should give their money away while still alive. For 10 points, name this steel tycoon who funded thousands of libraries.

tossups.p: This man’s family left Dunfermline [“dun-FERM-lin”], Scotland, for Pennsylvania when he was 12, and his first job was as a bobbin boy in a cotton mill. Next he delivered messages for a telegraph office in Pittsburgh.
tossups.r: He later became one of the richest people in the world. For 10 points, name this steel tycoon who wrote _The Gospel of Wealth_.

tossups.p: This man named his first steel mill, the Edgar Thomson Works, after a railroad president he hoped would buy his rails. His company became a model of vertical integration, owning its own iron ore mines, coal fields, railroads, and ships.
tossups.r: His partner Henry Clay Frick first got rich selling coke, a fuel made from coal. For 10 points, name this Pittsburgh steel tycoon.

tossups.p: This man supported heavy taxes on large estates and wrote that “the man who dies thus rich dies disgraced.” He first published those ideas in an 1889 essay titled simply “Wealth” in the _North American Review_.
tossups.r: That essay became known as _The Gospel of Wealth_. For 10 points, name this philanthropist who made his fortune in steel.

tossups.p: In 1900, this man founded technical schools in Pittsburgh that later merged with an institute started by the family of banker Andrew Mellon. That school is now a university that bears both men’s names.
tossups.r: His partner Henry Clay Frick hired Pinkerton guards during the Homestead Strike. For 10 points, name this Scottish-born steel tycoon.

tossups.p: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky [“chy-KOFF-skee”] conducted at the opening festival of a New York concert hall, paid for by this man, that opened in 1891. This man also funded an institution for scientific research in Washington, D.C.
tossups.r: He made his fortune in steel and gave much of it away. For 10 points, name this philanthropist, the namesake of that famous concert hall.

tossups.p: This immigrant praised his adopted country’s progress in the 1886 book _Triumphant Democracy_. Critics called him a “robber baron,” while admirers saw this self-made man, who once worked in a cotton mill, as a “captain of industry.”
tossups.r: He sold his steel company to J.P. Morgan in 1901. For 10 points, name this Gilded Age tycoon who gave away most of his fortune.

clues.t: Scottish-born steel tycoon (1835–1919) who built his fortune in Pittsburgh
Philanthropist who gave away most of his fortune, funding more than 2,500 public libraries
Sold his steel company to J.P. Morgan in 1901 for about $480 million; Morgan made it the heart of U.S. Steel
His name is on a New York concert hall (opened 1891) and on a Pittsburgh university now shared with Andrew Mellon
Wrote _The Gospel of Wealth_ (1889): the rich should use their fortunes to help society
The Homestead Strike (1892) at his Pennsylvania steel plant ended in a deadly battle
His partner Henry Clay Frick ran the company and fought the union
Frick hired Pinkerton guards to break the Homestead Strike while the boss was away in Scotland
Left Dunfermline, Scotland, at 12 (1848); worked as a bobbin boy in a cotton mill, then as a telegraph messenger
Used vertical integration: his company owned its own iron ore mines, coal fields, railroads, and ships
Opened the Edgar Thomson Works (1875), using the Bessemer process to make cheap steel
Critics called him a “robber baron”; admirers called him a “captain of industry”
Founded the Keystone Bridge Company (1865), which built James Eads’s bridge at St. Louis (1874)
Mentor Thomas A. Scott hired him at the Pennsylvania Railroad; in the Civil War he helped run Union military railroads and telegraphs
_The Gospel of Wealth_ opens by calling “the proper administration of wealth” the “problem of our age”
“The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced”; he also backed heavy taxes on large estates
Charles M. Schwab negotiated the 1901 sale; U.S. Steel became the first billion-dollar corporation
Opposed taking over the Philippines and offered $20 million so it could buy its independence
Founded an Endowment for International Peace (1910) and the Church Peace Union; paid for the Peace Palace in The Hague
Paid for a new library in Johnstown after the 1889 Johnstown Flood; towns had to supply the land and upkeep for his libraries
“Dippy,” a _Diplodocus_ skeleton, belongs to a species named for him; he sent copies to museums around the world
Created a Hero Fund (1904) for people who risk their lives to save others
Wrote _Triumphant Democracy_ (1886), praising his adopted country
Funded a science institution in Washington, D.C.; Tchaikovsky conducted at his New York concert hall’s opening festival (1891)

trap.title: Which Carnegie built what?
trap.body: Lots of things carry the Carnegie name: Carnegie Hall, Carnegie Mellon University, and Dale Carnegie, the self-help author of _How to Win Friends and Influence People_, who was no relation. Players also mix up the Gilded Age tycoons: his partner Henry Clay Frick, oil king John D. Rockefeller, and banker J.P. Morgan. One real question even calls Carnegie the founder of U.S. Steel, but J.P. Morgan formed U.S. Steel in 1901 by buying Carnegie’s company.
trap.fix: Steel, Pittsburgh, Homestead, _The Gospel of Wealth_, and libraries mean Andrew Carnegie. Oil and Standard Oil mean Rockefeller; banking and creating U.S. Steel mean Morgan; the man who hired the Pinkertons is Frick.
trap.line: Real answer line: Andrew Carnegie (the same plain line in all 8 real tossups)
